title: Why Philanthropy is Silent in the Golden Age of Wealth — TikTok
notes: Hook question: with record wealth at the top and government funding cut, why is American giving at an all-time low? Answer, built scene by scene: everyday donors dropped out, even the affluent give less, the tax code rewards the richest givers most, today's billionaires give far less than Gilded Age titans, and nonprofits are left at risk. The close names the fix: reform tax incentives and fund the common interest collectively.

All figures are from the article (Apr 29, 2026) and the sources it cites (Bank of America, Giving USA, Center for Effective Philanthropy, Urban Institute, Lilly Family School). Co-authored post, so the narration uses 'we'.

post.headline: Billionaires are giving less than ever
post.caption: American wealth is at a record high, but philanthropy has hit an all-time low. Twenty years ago nearly two-thirds of households gave to charity, and today just 41% do, while 61% of nonprofits say their survival is at risk.
post.cta: Full story and interactive charts at the link in bio.

say: Trump era tax cuts make it easier for wealthy households to accumulate wealth without the incentive to donate more. A $1,000 donation for someone in the 35% bracket now saves $350, but not long ago it would save $500 for the top marginal tax bracket.

cues.text: Despite record-breaking wealth in America, philanthropy has now hit record-breaking lows.
At a time when government is cutting social services, elites are also pulling back from donations, leaving low-income communities reeling.
We looked at why those with the deepest pockets are retreating to the sidelines.
Without donations and government grants, most nonprofits in the US would run at a loss. Nonprofits in Louisiana would be hardest hit of any state.
But the data reveals that in 2015 91% of affluent households gave to charity. Now, this has fallen to 81%.
Charities rely heavily on big donors. In 2024, donors giving over $50,000 accounted for nearly 78% of total funds given to charities.
Everyday donors have retreated too. Nearly two-thirds of households gave twenty years ago. Today, it is just 41%.
Dollars aren't the only thing disappearing. 50% of affluent households volunteered their time in 2015. Today, only 43% volunteer. For the general public, it's lower still, at just 28%.
The tax code rewards the richest givers, since a $1,000 deduction saves $120 in the 12% bracket and $350 in the 35% bracket.
It's a stark departure from the Gilded Age, when Carnegie, Rockefeller, and Mellon felt obligated to give, building thousands of libraries and cultural centers.
Today's richest, like Bezos, Musk and Zuckerberg, have given away a fraction of their wealth, sometimes as low as 1/100th.
Who gives shapes what gets funded, as wealthy donors favor universities and the arts while everyday donors fund food banks.
Now 61% of nonprofits say their survival is at risk, while 87% of foundations report rising demand.
Philanthropy is being asked to fill gaps in public systems that desperately need help, but those elite donors aren't answering the call.
We need to reform tax incentives and fund the common interest instead of relying on a few billionaires who ebb and flow in their support of public needs.
You can read the full story on American Inequality.
